James John Smith was born on the 1st of January, 2009.

From the very beginning, it was clear to any casual observers that James was a rather special child. "Special" is a word which parents regularly used to describe their newborn children; indeed, it would be rather unusual for any child, at any point in its life, to not have been described as special by its blind and doting parents. James, however, was special even by the standards of the most impartial of observers with but a clinical, detached interest in infants.

You see, when parents say that their children are special, what they typically mean to imply is that their children are possess one or two traits that they hope - or if they're particularly foolish, that they unabashedly believe - will lead them on to great achievement and renown. It is for this reason that parents of grotesquely deformed children rarely if ever call their children special, and for the same reason that the most bog-standard, average, and even mildly unintelligent child will be deemed "special" for having developed at the age of three months old an interest in chewing on crayons (which, for some unfathomable reason, has indicated to more than one set of overly-hopeful parents that their son will become the next Picasso).

No, James was not special in that he possessed any outstanding traits, imagined or not. He was not outstandingly intelligent, nor was he outstandingly strong; he was not outstandingly handsome, nor was he outstandingly charming; inasmuch as freshly-born babies could be any of the above, at any rate.

No, if James' peculiarities had to be put into words, he would perhaps be best described as "determined, and lucky".

At first glance, that description appears to consist of two completely separate traits. But the truth is that with James, determination and good fortune appeared to come hand in hand; allow me to illustrate this by an anecdote from when he was nine months old.

At the age of nine months, James had just learnt to walk unaided. This in itself is not a particularly outstanding achievement - indeed, by some metrics James would have been considered a slow learner. But it is nonetheless important to consider in the back of your mind, for it will soon illustrate the sheer unlikelihood of what happened next to have unfolded on nothing more than the whims of Lady Luck.
